findings.title: Device limit can be bypassed by retrying after a rejected device because the local cache is populated before the limit check succeeds
findings.body: In tagDeviceUI, the device key is added to localCache before a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice propagates the error and the anonymous authentication fails, but the cache entry remains valid for 29 minutes. A subsequent request from the same device ID hits the cached value at the top of tagDeviceUI and returns nil without consulting the device limit, so authentication succeeds. A client can intentionally send two requests: the first triggers the limit and the second is allowed, defeating the configurable device limit. Cache the device only after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or delete the cache entry on error.

findings.title: Device limit can be exceeded under concurrent requests because count and insert/update are not atomic
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first calls CountDevices to check whether the current count is below deviceLimit, then performs a later INSERT/UPDATE outside any transaction or lock. Concurrent authentication attempts for different new device IDs can all observe count < deviceLimit and all proceed to insert, pushing the total above the configured limit. In a multi-instance Grafana deployment this race is realistic. The count-and-insert/update pair should be performed in a transaction with appropriate locking, or otherwise made atomic, to actually enforce the limit.

findings.title: Anonymous authentication now synchronously performs database work for device tagging
findings.body: The previous implementation tagged anonymous devices in a goroutine with a separate timeout, keeping the authentication hot path independent of the anon_device database table. This change moves TagDevice into the synchronous Authenticate path. On a local-cache miss, tagDeviceUI executes a COUNT query on anon_device followed by an INSERT/UPDATE before authentication completes. A burst of first-time device IDs, a large anon_device table, or a slow/unavailable database will add latency to anonymous sign-in, and the request context will be consumed by that database work. If the limit must be enforced synchronously, consider a cheaper or transactional enforcement mechanism that does not couple every new anonymous session to a multi-query database round trip.
